title: Evaluation of Partially Automated Driving HMI with Driver Monitoring in Simulation
author: Schömig, Kremer, et al.
materials: For each use case in drive B it is recommended to describe the actions the experimenter has to do to bring the system into the required start state for this use case (either the instruction what the subject is told to do, e.g. press button XY, or the how the state should be trigged via the simulation software). Furthermore, the use case should contain the sequence of questions that have to be asked together with predefined answer categories that allow to directly classify the answers as correct or false. The protocol should also allow to write down alternative not foreseen answers. In the best case, the test protocol is designed in a way that the relevant self-report and behavioral can directly be coded as correct or false.

steps.title: Prepare comprehensive test protocol
steps.instruction: Create a written protocol that contains all information needed for the study: pre‑drive instructions, in‑drive instructions, the ordered list of use cases for each drive, simulation software inputs for triggering system states, exact timing of each trigger, the self‑report questions, and the behavioral indicators to be observed.

steps.title: Define Drive A use cases
steps.instruction: For every use case in Drive A specify the start and end points on the route, the behavioral categories that allow the experimenter to classify observed driver behavior as correct or incorrect, and the exact time point and action required to trigger any system state.

substeps.instruction: List behavioral categories (e.g., timely speed adaptation after speed‑limit change).
Specify trigger time and action for each required system state.

steps.title: Conduct Drive A and record behavior
steps.instruction: During Drive A follow the sequence of use cases, trigger system states at the pre‑defined times, and observe driver actions, classifying each observed behavior immediately as correct or incorrect according to the predefined categories; note any additional driver remarks.

steps.title: Interview participants after Drive A
steps.instruction: After Drive A have the experimenter fill an interview sheet with the participant’s answers to: (1) which system they were driving (classify as correct L2, incorrect L1 or L3), and (2) predefined questions about reasons for any inadequate behavior; probe further if the answer is ambiguous, and record any unexpected answers separately.

substeps.instruction: Mark system identification as L2, L1, or L3.
If answer is unclear, ask more specific follow‑up questions.
Do not label behavior as inadequate unless a wrong mental model is confirmed.

steps.title: Define Drive B use cases
steps.instruction: For each use case in Drive B describe the actions the experimenter must perform to bring the system into the required start state (subject instruction such as “press button XY” or simulation‑software trigger), list the sequence of self‑report questions with predefined answer categories that allow direct classification as correct or false, and provide a field for unforeseen answers.

substeps.instruction: List self‑report questions and answer categories.

steps.title: Conduct Drive B and record responses
steps.instruction: Execute Drive B according to the prepared use‑case list, trigger the start‑state actions, ask the predefined questions during each use case, and code each self‑report and observed behavior immediately as correct or false.

steps.title: Adapt protocol to system specifics
steps.instruction: Modify the protocol as needed: omit use cases that the investigated system does not support (e.g., no automatic speed adaptation or missing hands‑off/eyes‑off DMS), adjust behavioral categories for Drive A (e.g., “timely speed adaptation after speed‑limit change”), and adjust answer categories for Drive B to match the HMI outputs used to indicate system state.

steps.title: Recruit participant sample
steps.instruction: Enroll at least 20 naïve subjects (over‑recruit to ensure 20 valid data sets per HMI/DMS condition), distributed evenly across four age groups (18‑24, 25‑39, 40‑54, 55 +), and aim for an approximate 50:50 gender balance; ensure all participants have similar, limited prior experience with assistance systems.

substeps.instruction: Calculate required over‑recruitment to reach 20 valid datasets.
Select participants to meet the age‑group quotas.

steps.title: Set up driving simulator
steps.instruction: Configure a driving simulator that implements L2 longitudinal and lateral control based on simulated sensors, includes a DMS with hands‑on sensors and/or eye‑tracking cameras, follows the real‑system state diagram, and provides all HMI outputs (visual cluster/HUD/LED, auditory sounds/speech, haptic seat vibrations). Ensure the simulator can display a bird‑eye view of the environment, a driver‑face view, and a view of HMI elements and hand positions.

substeps.instruction: Load the system state diagram with all transitions.
Add visual, auditory, and haptic output channels.
Set up multi‑view displays (environment, driver face, HMI).

steps.title: Run simulation study
steps.instruction: With the prepared protocol, recruited participants, and configured simulator, conduct the full study: run Drive A, perform the post‑Drive A interview, run Drive B, collect all self‑report and behavioral data, and store them for later analysis of the seven L2‑HMI requirements.
